newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi's military ruler takes oath of office.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's military ruler takes oath of office.

text.p: Burundi's military ruler took a solemn oath of office on Friday promising to make all efforts to ensure stability and peace.
But Pierre Buyoya did not swear allegiance to Burundi's constitution, which he suspended after taking power in the central African country in late July.

Buyoya, a retired major, pledged before leaders of the military, judiciary and civil society that he would follow his obligations in terms of a transitional decree issued after the army threw out president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya on July 25.
"We are committed to organising a national debate. Preparations are under way," he told a crowd gathered in the main auditorium of a university campus on a hill overlooking the capital.
"We reaffirm our commitment that talks will be held with armed groups," said Buyoya, who was dressed in a dark suit.

He has previously said Hutu rebels should reject the ideology of genocide and stop killing civilians, as part of a process leading to negotiations, but he made no mention of these moves in his speech.

He said the government was committed to dialogue with armed factions and was surprised that neighbouring countries, which have slapped economic sanctions on Burundi, doubted his government's sincerity on talks.
"Our wish is that armed groups would accept our offer of dialogue," he said after signing a register of office in front of seven judges in red robes with black and gold hats.
The ceremony ended with the officers rising and saluting as a military band played the national anthem on a lawn outside the entrance to the hall.
Burundi drummers, dressed in the red, green and white of the national flag, hammered at their drums before and after the proceedings, the beats echoing on the hills behind.

Buyoya has lifted a ban on political parties and announced the restoration of the national assembly and his government has repeatedly appealed to be unshackled from an economic embargo that has cut oil and other vital supplies for nearly two months.
The boycott on the landlocked state has also stopped exports of coffee and tea, the country's major cash earners.

A committee of African countries overseeing the sanctions recommended on Thursday that Buyoya "be invited to be available" for the next regional summit to discuss the situation in Burundi, where ethnic war has killed at least 150,000 majority Hutus and minority Tutsis since 1993.

Buyoya and the Tutsi-dominated army have not held talks with the main Hutu rebels led by Leonard Nyangoma, who have condemned his take-over as the work of "putschists". The military ruler has promised a three-year transitional period, which began when he took power, saying he was trying to head off genocide.

Many people fear that Burundi could go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda, which has a similar ethnic mix. Up to a million people, mainly Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were killed in fighting and genocidal massacres there in 1994.
